The student is subject to mandatory withdrawal because her total absence reached 21%, exceeding the policy’s 20% threshold. The 6 percentage points covered by the properly stamped medical excuse do not reduce the relevant count: the Medical Excuses rule expressly provides that the period on a stamped medical excuse is counted in the student’s “20% for absence with an excuse.” Under Attendance Policy clause A, withdrawal is mandatory when absence reaches 20%. A forced withdrawal results in a “W” under clause B. Because the excuse covered a final-exam period, it also falls under Medical Excuses clause (a), which requires submission of the approved medical report to the college when the excuse includes a final exam or other graded work.

The appeal cannot be conclusively classified from the facts given. Article Seven of the Student Affairs Regulations allows an appeal within 30 days after the student is notified of the penalty. If the announcement of results was also notification of the penalty, filing on day 32 was two days late and outside the stated period. If results were not the penalty notification, the evidence does not establish when the 30-day period began. Article Eighteen provides that Student Affairs Committee decisions are not altered after Presidential approval, except in the case of student appeals.

answer:
The student begins at 12 credit hours, which is the stated maximum for a student on academic probation. Probation restricts registration to 12 hours per regular semester, and the academic advisor’s recommendation is mandatory for selecting the courses (Student Handbook; Registration Procedures—Academic probation).

A drop-and-add would have to comply with the announced add/drop dates and all registration rules. The evidence does not state whether adding a course after week 2 is within the announced period, so that timing cannot be confirmed from the retrieved regulations. Article 7(b) requires that the registered hours not exceed the permitted maximum or fall below the minimum; the general minimum is 9 hours under Article 8(b). If the student drops one course and adds another of equal credit value, the final load remains 12 hours. She cannot have more than 12 registered hours at any point while on probation. If the drop occurs first, her interim load may be 9 hours, but the replacement course must still be approved and validly registered.

The prerequisite issue is decisive. Article 8(f) provides that a student may not register for a course unless its prerequisites have been completed, except for a graduating student whose case is approved by the concerned college. Therefore, if the course being dropped is the prerequisite for the third course, the third course cannot ordinarily remain registered after that prerequisite is dropped; the student would need to drop or otherwise resolve the third course as well. The retrieved evidence contains no separate rule defining or permitting a “bundled” prerequisite exception.

Probation continues to affect the student’s registration: the 12-hour ceiling remains, and the GPA is reviewed after completion of every 12 credit hours (13 for the College of Maritime Transport and Technology). The evidence does not establish a special probation consequence merely because the change is made after week 2 or because a course is dropped, beyond compliance with the load, prerequisite, and add/drop rules.
cited_articles: Article 8(a) (general maximum load); Article 8(b) (minimum load of 9 hours); Article 8(f) (prerequisites); Article 7(b) (hours must remain within the permitted limits); Registration Procedures—“Students can drop or add a registered course during the announced dates while abiding by all registration rules and regulations”; Student Handbook—Academic Probation (12-credit-hour limit, advisor recommendation, and review after every 12 completed credit hours).
